analysis.title: Early Morning Reid - Macro Strategy
key_insights: S&P 500 fell 0.23% to 7324, its 5th consecutive decline. It is down 3.15% on the week, which if sustained would be the biggest weekly decline since the April 2025 Liberation Day tariff announcements. It is at a 5-month low and 6.33% below its October peak, the largest peak-to-trough decline since March.

The selloff has no single driver. Nvidia fell 2.89% after Tuesday's results, extending its decline from the early October peak to 37%. The NASDAQ (+0.42%) and Mag-7 (+0.50%) rebounded after four straight declines, so losses have broadened beyond tech.
A consistent pattern in recent days: a recovery in US equity futures early in the session is followed by fresh losses around the cash open. S&P 500 futures are +0.60% this morning.

Asia fell overnight. Hang Seng -1.83% is on course for its lowest level since June, CSI 300 -0.24% for its lowest since July 2025, and Shanghai Comp -0.29% for its lowest since August 2025. Nikkei +0.48% outperformed. ASX 200 fell 1.04% after Australian unemployment rose to a 5-year high of 4.9% in October (vs 4.7% expected).

The 10yr Treasury yield fell 3.8bps to 5.07% and is down another 1.6bps to 5.05% this morning, despite hawkish Fed Governor Waller comments earlier in the session. Waller said the Fed must be 'a little more aggressive in our rate hikes' and that if January is not signalled as a hike, a 50bp move in December would be needed.

Fed October minutes were hawkish: 'almost all participants' had a baseline that included higher rates, and 'a couple of participants' thought a hike larger than 25bps could warrant consideration at the next meeting if incoming inflation data were unfavorable. Further hikes were already priced, so the market reaction was small.

Commodities fell broadly on demand concerns. Brent -1.28% to $91.95/bbl, WTI -3.20% to $83.26/bbl, gold -3.23% to a 14-month low of $3,725/oz, metals -5.30% (largest daily decline since July 2025), corn -2.34%, wheat -3.97%. Brent is +0.21% to $92.14 this morning after a New York Times report that President Trump is considering further strikes on Iran, with no decision made.
Inflation expectations fell: the 1yr Euro inflation swap dropped 9.2bps to 3.00% and the 1yr US inflation swap dropped 5.0bps to 2.02%.

Deutsche's argument is that bearish risks are partly offsetting. Larger equity declines coincide with lower sovereign yields (easing fiscal stress) and lower inflation pressure (easing rate-hike concern), so the most bearish outcomes are unlikely to occur at once.

Europe: STOXX 600 fell 1.03% to a three-week low, its first back-to-back declines of more than 1% since March. EUR/USD fell 0.21% to $1.0975, its lowest close since April 2025. 10yr Bund yields fell 0.7bps, OATs 1.5bps, BTPs 0.4bps.

UK October CPI was 3.6% y/y headline, a 12-month high and in line with consensus, but below the BoE staff projection of 3.7%. The 10yr gilt yield fell 8.2bps to 5.29%, and rate hikes priced by September 2027 fell 6.8bps to 86bps. Sterling fell 0.45% to $1.3149, its weakest vs the dollar in almost a year.

Day ahead: US weekly jobless claims, Philadelphia Fed and Kansas City Fed manufacturing surveys, Walmart earnings. Fed speakers include Vice Chair Jefferson, Hammack, Goolsbee, Barr, Barkin and Paulson. ECB President Lagarde and the BoE's Dhingra also speak.
Adrian Cox published a Deutsche Bank Research Institute report arguing that India may be the best place to look for what AI can bring, and that adoption matters more than invention.

risk_factors: Broadening equity selloff beyond tech, with the S&P 500 on course for its largest weekly decline since April 2025.
AI-related slowdown fears centred on Nvidia and the AI investment boom.
Hawkish Fed risk: Waller flagged a possible 50bp hike in December, and minutes show a couple of participants open to a hike larger than 25bps.
Weakening demand: broad commodity declines and a rising Australian unemployment rate.
Intraday reversals: US futures recoveries have repeatedly faded at the cash open.

tension_points.bull_case: Bearish risks offset each other. As equities fall on AI slowdown fears, sovereign bond yields fall (easing fiscal stress) and inflation pressure declines (easing concern about rate hikes), so it is difficult for all the most bearish outcomes to happen at once.
tension_points.bear_case: The selloff has broadened beyond tech, the S&P 500 has fallen five sessions in a row, and the Fed is signalling more hikes, with Waller flagging a possible 50bp move in December.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Fed Governor Waller said that without a January hike signal, 'you have to go 50 in December'. A larger hike or hawkish inflation data would undercut the offset argument.

theme_stances.key_argument: Falling yields and inflation pressure partly offset the equity selloff, so the most bearish outcomes are unlikely to occur at once.
